title: Service Discovery & Configuration
subtitle: Locate healthy service instances and change runtime behavior without unsafe fleet-wide assumptions
objectives: Separate logical service names from changing instance addresses
Reason about discovery freshness and health
Roll out configuration with validation and rollback
Use feature flags without creating permanent hidden branches

exercises.title: Service discovery maps a stable logical name to a changing set of reachable instances
exercises.body: Application code targets a logical service identity while a discovery mechanism returns current endpoints. Registration, health, and expiry remove replaced instances so deployments and failures do not require callers to embed machine addresses.
exercises.note: DNS, a registry, or a platform control plane can provide discovery; the required freshness and routing behavior determine the mechanism.

exercises.prompt: Checkout embeds Inventory Server A's address. A deployment replaces A with Servers B and C, and checkout keeps calling the dead address.
choices: Commit B's address into checkout source code
choiceFeedback: The next replacement recreates the same coupling and requires another caller deployment.
The stable name resolves to the current healthy endpoint set.
Retries cannot make a retired address healthy and consume the request deadline.
exercises.beforeStatus: DEPLOYMENT · inventory address changed · checkout unavailable
exercises.afterStatus: DEPLOYMENT · discovery returns B and C · checkout continues
exercises.result: Caller configuration no longer depends on one instance address
exercises.why: A logical service name separates caller configuration from instance lifecycle. Discovery still needs bounded caching and endpoint expiry so clients do not retain removed addresses indefinitely.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: Checkout embeds Inventory Server A's address. A deployment replaces A with Servers B and C, and checkout keeps calling the dead address. Place inventory.service, Servers B + C. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Checkout → inventory.service; inventory.service → Servers B + C. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A logical service name separates caller configuration from instance lifecycle. Discovery still needs bounded caching and endpoint expiry so clients do not retain removed addresses indefinitely.

exercises.prompt: Match each discovery model to where endpoint selection occurs.

pairs.right: Caller selects an endpoint from the registry result
A proxy or load balancer selects the endpoint
Name resolution returns one or more addresses

exercises.why: Client-side discovery puts selection logic in callers, server-side discovery centralizes it in an intermediary, and DNS uses standard name resolution with cache behavior governed by TTLs and resolvers.

exercises.prompt: Why must a discovery record expire or be actively deregistered?
choices: A dead instance cannot reliably remove itself, so stale endpoints otherwise remain routable
exercises.why: A crashed process cannot announce its own death. Leases, health observations, and bounded TTLs let the control plane remove endpoints that stop renewing or serving successfully.

exercises.title: Discovery health must reflect the operation a caller needs
exercises.body: Liveness asks whether a process should be restarted; readiness asks whether it should receive traffic. A ready endpoint must have the dependencies and local state required for the advertised operation, while checks need thresholds that avoid removing instances during brief noise.
exercises.note: One global health result can be too coarse when reads remain safe but writes require an unavailable dependency.

exercises.prompt: A new instance registers before loading its routing table. It returns errors for 40 seconds while receiving production traffic.
choices: Register only after required state is loaded and remove readiness before shutdown
Ignore the errors during every deployment
choiceFeedback: Process existence does not prove the instance can serve its advertised operation.
Readiness aligns endpoint visibility with the instance's ability to handle traffic.
Expected errors still consume capacity and harm users.
exercises.beforeStatus: ROLLOUT · unready instance receives 25% traffic · errors
exercises.afterStatus: ROLLOUT · instance joins after state load · zero warm-up traffic errors
exercises.why: Readiness registration prevents traffic before required initialization completes. During shutdown, removing readiness and allowing in-flight requests to drain reduces connection resets and partial work.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A new instance registers before loading its routing table. It returns errors for 40 seconds while receiving production traffic. Place Ready, Load balancer. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: New instance → Ready; Ready → Load balancer. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Readiness registration prevents traffic before required initialization completes. During shutdown, removing readiness and allowing in-flight requests to drain reduces connection resets and partial work.

exercises.prompt: Which signals can justify removing an endpoint from routing? Select all.
choices: The deployment intentionally begins draining it
One unrelated user mistypes a password
exercises.why: Repeated readiness failure, expired registration, and intentional drain all indicate that new traffic should stop. A valid application-level rejection such as a bad password does not mean the endpoint is unhealthy.

exercises.prompt: Instances fail quickly, but one-second network blips are common. Choose the health-removal emphasis.
exercises.rightLabel: Require repeated failure with a short threshold
exercises.why: A short repeated-failure threshold balances detection time against false eviction from transient loss. The exact count and interval follow failure cost, fleet headroom, and observed network noise.

lessons.title: Drain traffic as an instance degrades

exercises.title: Health changes routing before they change membership
exercises.body: An instance may still answer probes while its safe capacity falls. Outlier detection or readiness can drain new traffic gradually, leaving only a bounded share while connections finish. Immediate deletion and continued full routing are not the only choices.
exercises.note: The registry advertises candidates; the client or load balancer still applies health and freshness policy.

exercises.prompt: An instance now safely handles only 1,000 of the fleet's 10,000 req/s. Drag the *smallest* share drained to healthy instances that keeps the degraded instance alive.
exercises.why: Draining 90% leaves 1,000 requests/sec on the degraded instance, exactly its current safe capacity. A production policy normally preserves headroom and eventually removes it when readiness or lease state says it cannot serve.

exercises.title: Runtime configuration is a versioned production input
exercises.body: Configuration can change routing, limits, and feature behavior without a code deployment, so it needs schema validation, versioning, staged rollout, observability, and rollback. Services should expose which version they loaded and reject malformed values safely.
exercises.note: A feature flag is temporary configuration with ownership and an expiry plan; stale flags create untested execution branches.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: Runtime configuration is a versioned production input
exercises.why: Configuration can change routing, limits, and feature behavior without a code deployment, so it needs schema validation, versioning, staged rollout, observability, and rollback. Services should expose which version they loaded and reject malformed values safely. A feature flag is temporary configuration with ownership and an expiry plan; stale flags create untested execution branches.

steps: Validate the new configuration against its schema and constraints
Apply it to a small canary population
Compare user and system metrics with the control population
Expand gradually or roll back to the previous version
exercises.why: Validation catches malformed input, immutable versions make state identifiable, a canary limits blast radius, and comparative evidence determines expansion or rollback.

exercises.prompt: Which properties should a production feature flag have? Select all.
choices: Expected removal date or permanent-policy decision
A different undocumented default in every service
exercises.why: Ownership, lifecycle, and exposure evidence keep a flag operable and removable. Divergent undocumented defaults make behavior depend on which service instance receives a request.

exercises.prompt: Build a configuration path that supports staged rollout and rollback.
exercises.why: The version store preserves validated immutable configurations, and the rollout controller selects which population receives each version. Keeping the previous version enables an explicit rollback rather than another emergency edit.

exercises.prompt: A canary configuration is safe on 1% of instances but breaks at 50%. What rollout mechanism limits blast radius?
choices: Versioned staged rollout with health gates and rollback
exercises.why: A staged rollout exposes a small cohort, evaluates explicit health signals, and advances only when evidence remains acceptable. Versioning supports deterministic rollback.
